sec.title: EEG results: Neural reactivation of bridge element during the choice phase predicts successful inference but is unaffected by stress or retrieval practice
sec.p: As a complementary control analysis, we examined the choice phase to determine whether bridge-related category reactivation was specific to the initial inference period or also present during the later response-selection period. This analysis addressed whether the stress- and retrieval-practice effects observed during the cue/inference period generalized to the subsequent choice phase. Because participants selected their response during this 3-s window, this analysis was interpreted cautiously and was not used as the primary neural test of inference-related reactivation. Applying the same multivariate decoder to the choice phase—during which participants viewed the cue (A) alongside the potential target (C)—revealed significant reactivation of the bridge element across all conditions (Figure 3B). Cluster-based permutation tests on the decoding time course identified three significant temporal clusters: two early cluster from 330–480 ms、580–1110 (p<.05) and a more sustained later cluster from 2030–2660 ms (p<.05). To quantify this effect, we extracted the mean decoding accuracy within these time windows and investigated its functional relevance: this choice-phase reactivation of the bridge element was significantly greater on successfully inferred trials compared to unsuccessful trials (t(133) = 2.92, p = 0.004, Cohen’s d = 0.25, 95% CI =[0.56, 2.94]).

Crucially, in a key divergence from the initial inference period, this choice-phase reactivation was not modulated by interaction between acute stress and retrieval practice. We formally tested this using two complementary metrics. First, a 2 (Stress: Stress vs. No-Stress) × 2 (Session: Retrieval Practice vs. No-Retrieval Practice). ANOVA on overall decodability yielded no significant interaction between Stress and Retrieval Practice (F(1,132)=0.01, p=0.94, ηp2<0.001; Figure 6C). A second parallel one ANOVA on mean decoding accuracy yielded also no significant interaction (F(1,132) = 0.35, p = 0.56, ηp2 = 0.003; Figure 6D). In sum, while bridge element reactivation occurs during the choice phase and predicts performance, this neural signal—unlike the rapid reactivation during the initial inference stage—showed no interaction between Stress and Retreival Practice.

sec.title: EEG results: Theta oscillations analyses are consistent with behavioral and reactivation patterns
sec.p: To complement our behavioral and neural reactivation findings, we performed time-frequency analyses focusing on theta oscillations to further elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying the effects of stress on memory inference. Given the established role of theta oscillations in memory integration, we hypothesized that theta power during the inference task would also be modulated by acute stress and that retrieval practice would mitigate this effect. In Experiment 1, a cluster-based permutation test comparing the control and stress groups revealed a significant stress-induced reduction in theta power (Control > Stress). This effect was isolated to a single late-emerging cluster, spanning from 1680 ms to 4000 ms relative to cue onset (p = 0.007; Figure 7A). The corresponding time-frequency map of T-values across an extended 2–12 Hz frequency range confirms this result, showing a concentration of positive T-values within the theta band during this significant time window, indicative of higher power in the control group (Figure 7B). In contrast, for Experiment 2, no significant clusters were found in the same comparison between control and stress groups, suggesting that retrieval practice prevented the stress-induced suppression of theta power. To directly test the influence of retrieval practice, we performed a non-parametric cluster-based permutation test comparing participants from Experiment 2 (retrieval practice) with those from Experiment 1 (no retrieval practice). This analysis revealed that retrieval practice was associated with significantly higher theta power within two early time windows post-cue onset: 40–380 ms (p < 0.001) and 520–900 ms (p = 0.021) (Figure 7C and 7D). Taken together, these results suggest that acute stress impairs theta-band activity associated with later stages of memory inference, and that retrieval practice can prevent this deficit by boosting theta-related processing during the initial phase of inference.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our study shows that acute stress is associated with impaired memory-based inference and reduced rapid bridge-related reactivation. We demonstrate that this impairment is preventable through retrieval practice, which restores both behavioral performance and underlying neural reactivations. Using multivariate decoding of EEG data, we identified the rapid reactivation of the bridge element (B) as a critical predictor of successful inference (A-C). This reactivation process was specifically attenuated by stress but was robustly restored—and even enhanced—by retrieval practice. These findings provide a novel neuroscientific account of how memory inference is accomplished, clarify its vulnerability to stress, and highlight a powerful behavioral strategy for building stress resilience.

A central contribution of our work is the identification of rapid bridge-element reactivation as a core neural process for memory-based inference. While prior neuroimaging research has focused on the roles of the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex in integrating memories during encoding (Zeithamova and Preston, 2010; Zeithamova et al., 2012; Backus et al., 2016; Morton et al., 2020; Schlichting et al., 2021), our work elucidates the neural dynamics of the inference phase itself. We reveal that successful A-C inference is preceded by a rapid neural reactivation of the bridging element B. This extends prior decoding studies of deliberate retrieval or imagery (Polyn et al., 2005; Chadwick et al., 2010; Xue, 2018; Dijkstra et al., 2019). as the reactivation observed here appears to be a spontaneous, goal-relevant event essential for linking discrete memories. One consideration is that participants were informed of the A-C link via B on Day 2, which could encourage a deliberate reactivation. However, as these instructions were identical across all groups, they cannot account for the observed interaction between stress and retrieval practice, nor for the trial-by-trial relationship between reactivation strength and inference success. Future research could employ more implicit paradigms to disentangle the contributions of spontaneous versus goal-directed reactivation to memory inference.

Our results extend the literature on stress-induced memory retrieval deficits (de Quervain et al., 1998; Kuhlmann et al., 2005; Smeets, 2011; Shields et al., 2017; Wolf, 2017) to the domain of retrieval-dependent, more complex and constructive cognition. Consistent with the theoretical framework proposing that stress promotes a shift away from flexible, hippocampus-dependent cognitive strategies toward more rigid, striatum-based systems (Knowlton et al., 1996; Kluen et al., 2017b, 2017a; Raio et al., 2017; Vogel et al., 2018; Schwabe et al., 2022; Zerbes et al., 2022), we observed that acute stress impaired the retrieval of AB and BC associations and, in parallel, reduced the accuracy and speed of AC inference. While EEG lacks the spatial resolution to definitively dissociate hippocampal from striatal contributions, our data provide crucial temporal precision by showing that stress disrupts rapid reactivation of the bridge element B at the moment it is needed to support inference. We interpret this B reactivation as a retrieval operation that reactivates a shared mnemonic representation linking related events, which in turn enables the construction of the indirect AC relationship. An alternative interpretation is that stress impairs the retrieval of A-C associations that were spontaneously formed during encoding (Zhou et al., 2023). However, the trial-by-trial relationship between B reactivation and subsequent inference success, as well as the modulation of both behavioral and neural measures by retrieval practice, are more naturally explained by an online reactivation process that supports inference. Importantly, because stress also impaired retrieval of AB and BC pairs, our data cannot fully disentangle a general retrieval deficit from a more specific disruption of inferential integration. We therefore conclude that acute stress disrupts retrieval processes that are critical for memory-based inference, and that targeted retrieval practice can strengthen these stress-sensitive reactivation mechanisms to render subsequent inference more resilient.

Our study identifies retrieval practice (RP) as a potent countermeasure to the detrimental effects of acute stress on memory inference. Building on extensive evidence that RP strengthens memory (Karpicke and Blunt, 2011; Roediger and Butler, 2011; Liu et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Zhuang et al., 2021; Carpenter et al., 2022), we show that practicing the AB and BC pairs rendered the novel A-C inference resilient to stress. T This generalization of the testing effect to a novel, integrative inference task contrasts with prior findings where its benefits are often contingent on congruence between practice and test formats (Smith et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2020). Notably, retrieval practice did not enhance inference performance in the non-stress condition; instead, its benefit was to build resilience against acute stress, maintaining performance at levels equivalent to the non-stress group. This specific pattern of results supports an “online” inference mechanism. If A-C associations had been pre-compiled and stored during encoding, RP would likely have directly enhanced them, boosting performance regardless of stress. Therefore, we propose that the protective effect of RP transcends the reinforcement of individual associations. Instead, it fortifies the underlying relational memory structure, ensuring that the neural processes supporting inference—such as the rapid reactivation of the bridge element—remain robust against acute stress.

How does retrieval practice confer this stress resilience at the neural level? We propose that practicing retrieval of the AB and BC pairs serves to “tag” the entire ABC memory structure for subsequent offline consolidation (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013), potentially through co-reactivation during practice or subsequent sleep (Lutz et al., 2024). This mechanism is constrained by our data: retrieval practice did not significantly enhance A-C inference in the non-stress group. This specific pattern suggests that its benefit is not derived from strengthening a direct A-C link before the test. Instead, we argue that retrieval practice reinforces the relational integrity of the ABC structure, making the online reactivation of the bridge element more robust and thus more resilient to disruption by acute stress. Intriguingly, retrieval practice did more than simply restore bridge-element reactivation under stress; it upregulated this neural signal. The decoding strength for element B was highest in the RP-Stress group, significantly surpassing that of the RP-No Stress group. We interpret this heightened reactivation as a compensatory neural mechanism. When faced with the challenge of acute stress, the brain appears to amplify the critical neural process supporting inference. This interpretation aligns with broader theories of cognitive effort, which posit that additional neural resources are recruited to preserve performance in situations such as aging (Reuter-Lorenz and Cappell, 2008), facing increased task difficulty (Gray et al., 2003), or physiological challenges such as stress (Hermans et al., 2014).

To supplement our primary multivariate decoding results from the inference phase, we conducted two additional analyses of the EEG data. First, we applied the same decoder to the choice phase following inference. While this analysis also detected neural reactivation of the bridge element that predicted subsequent choice accuracy, this reactivation was notably not modulated by acute stress. We propose that this later reactivation is cognitively distinct from that observed during the initial inference process, likely reflecting post-inferential mechanisms such as choice confirmation rather than the act of inference itself. This dissociation suggest the time-specific effect of acute stess: it selectively disrupts neural reactivation during the cognitively demanding period of memory inference. Secondly, guided by the established role of theta oscillations in human memory (Herweg et al., 2020), and particularly in associative inference (Backus et al., 2016), we analyzed how stress and retrieval practice modulated theta-band activity. Acute stress selectively impaired theta power during the later stages of memory inference. In contrast, retrieval practice not only prevented this stress-induced deficit but also enhanced theta-band activity during the initial phase of inference. The modulation of theta oscillations thus corroborates our neural reactivation findings. Crucially, these time-frequency results provide valuable temporal information, pinpointing a later disruptive effect of stress and an earlier facilitative effect of retrieval practice on the underlying neural mechanisms.

Our study is not without limitations, which highlight key directions for future investigation. First, although we used well-established stimulus categories (i.e., faces, scenes, objects), the generalizability of our findings could be further tested using materials with greater ecological validity or semantic complexity. Second, the limited spatial resolution of EEG prevented us from identifying the precise anatomical sources of the reactivation signals. Future studies employing methods with higher spatial resolution are needed to elucidate the network-level interactions between the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and other relevant regions during stress-impaired inference. Third, while our findings demonstrate a clear protective benefit of retrieval practice, a valuable direction for future research would be to include a re-study control group. Such a design would allow for a precise dissociation of the cognitive mechanisms attributable to active retrieval versus those stemming from mere re-exposure to the material, further clarifying the unique role of retrieval in building stress-resilient inferential memories. Nonetheless, a substantial body of literature has established the superiority of retrieval practice over restudy for enhancing long-term retention (Roediger and Butler, 2011; Roediger and Abel, 2022) and building stress-resilient memories (Smith et al., 2016), providing a strong rationale for our interpretation. In addition, the post-inference direct-memory test used a two-alternative forced-choice format, which provides only a coarse measure of premise-memory strength and allows some correct responses to arise from guessing. Therefore, restricting analyses to trials in which both AB and BC pairs were later answered correctly does not guarantee that those trials were supported by strong associative memories. Future studies using cued recall, confidence ratings, or continuous measures of premise-memory strength would provide a more sensitive test of how premise memory supports later inference. A further limitation is that retrieval practice was implemented in a separate follow-up experiment rather than within a single fully crossed 2 × 2 factorial design. Although the two experiments were closely matched in recruitment procedures, participant population, laboratory setting, EEG system, task structure, and experimenter team, cohort-related confounds cannot be fully ruled out. Therefore, the cross-experiment stress-by-retrieval-practice analyses should be interpreted cautiously. Future studies using a fully crossed factorial design are needed to provide a more rigorous test of the interaction between retrieval practice and acute stress. Because retrieval practice was implemented as a brief free-recall task, we could not reliably link retrieval success for individual AB/BC associations to later A-C inference trials. Therefore, the present data do not allow a direct comparison of later inference performance for successfully versus unsuccessfully practiced items. The item-level mixed-effects analysis instead served as a robustness check and provided no indication that the primary behavioral pattern was driven by a small subset of ABC triads. Future studies using trial-by-trial cued retrieval practice will be needed to test item-specific retrieval-practice benefits more directly.Finally, pandemic-related safety protocols precluded cortisol collection, and future studies should integrate hormonal measures to provide a more comprehensive characterization of the stress response.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that acute stress impairs memory inference by disrupting the rapid neural reactivation of the shared bridge element that links related events. We identify this rapid reactivation as a critical neural computations underlying successful inference and pinpoint its disruption as a key mechanism through which stress impairs higher-order memory function. Critically, we show that retrieval practice was associated with attenuation of stress-induced inference impairment across two closely matched experiments. This protection is associated with the preservation and even enhancement of the underlying rapid reactivation signals. These findings elevate the role of retrieval practice from a simple tool for enhancing memory to a proactive strategy for building cognitive resilience, rendering complex memory functions against stress.

caption.title: Experimental procedures.
caption.p: (A) Encoding phase. Each trial began with a fixation cross (100 ms), followed by the presentation of an AB or BC image pair for 2500 ms. Each pair was presented twice, with the spatial positions reversed in the second presentation. (B) Retrieval practice phase. Following the encoding phase, participants were instructed to freely recall and fill in the blanks for the learned memory pairs (AB and BC) using paper and pen within a two-minute time limit. (C) Memory inference phase. Each trial started with a fixation point presented for a jittered duration (500, 1000, 1500, or 2000 ms), followed by a memory cue (Item A) for 4000 ms. Subsequently, three options were displayed, and participants were required to select the correct target (Item C) within 3000 ms. Distractors were images from the encoding phase (Day 1) that were not paired with the current cue. (D) Direct memory retrieval phase. After a jittered fixation, a cue (Item A or C) and two options (one being the correct Item B) were presented simultaneously. Participants had 3000 ms to make a selection. The distractor was a previously learned image from the same category as the correct option. (E) Localizer phase. Images were presented for 1500 ms with a 500 ms inter-trial interval. Participants performed a 1-back task, indicating whether the current image was identical to the preceding one.

body.p: This study presents valuable findings on how retrieval practice protects memory inferences from stress via covert memory reactivation. Via two EEG experiments manipulating stress and retrieval practice, the authors provide solid evidence showing that retrieval practice buffered negative impact of stress on behaviour and neural activities. This work will be of interest to cognitive and affective neuroscientists working on the intersection between memory and stress.
Summary:

The authors combine a two-day associative-inference task with EEG in two experiments involving 136 participants. Participants learn overlapping AB and BC pairs and subsequently infer AC relationships after a stress or control procedure. The second experiment adds retrieval practice after learning. Stress-related reductions in inference performance and bridge-category decoding in Experiment 1 are attenuated or reversed in Experiment 2.

The revision provides useful additional analyses and more explicit acknowledgment of the design's limitations. I no longer interpret Figure 4A as evidence of below-chance inference. However, several conclusions in the title, abstract, and Discussion remain stronger than the revised evidence supports.
Strengths:

The study addresses a worthwhile question by combining behavioral measures, an experimentally induced stress manipulation, and temporally resolved EEG. The independent visual localizer and decoding during the pre-choice period provide useful evidence that information related to the absent bridge category is available during inference.

Importantly, the evidence is not limited to a significant stress effect in one experiment and a nonsignificant effect in the other. The manuscript reports direct stress-by-experiment interactions for inference performance, response time, and decoding. The behavioral interaction also remains significant after adjustment for both-correct premise-triad counts. The exploratory mediation analysis, Bayesian comparison, and trial-level model improve the transparency of the evidence and deserve explicit credit.
Weaknesses:
(1) Premise memory strength and inference specific protection remain difficult to separate

The authors now acknowledge that strengthening AB/BC memories may contribute to better AC performance, and the exploratory mediation analysis supports this possibility. This is a useful clarification. However, a residual direct association after adjustment for premise memory does not establish an additional inference-specific mechanism. Premise memory was measured after inference using a coarse 2AFC test, and the mediation concerns the overall association with retrieval practice rather than specifically explaining the stress-by-practice interaction. Similarly, restricting analyses to both-correct trials or adjusting their number cannot equate underlying memory strength. The Discussion should therefore avoid treating the nonsignificant difference between the two control groups as evidence that the benefit transcends strengthened associations or specifically preserves online integration.
(2) The cross-experiment comparison supports an association with attenuation

The new interaction analyses strengthen the evidence that the stress effect differs between experiments. Nevertheless, retrieval practice was introduced in a separate follow-up cohort, so its effect remains confounded with experiment. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation; it should also guide the title and broader conclusions. "Associated with attenuation" is better supported than "prevents" or "restores." Likewise, the reported BF01 of 2.77 provides only weak support for no stress effect in Experiment 2 and does not establish equivalent performance. A randomized factorial study would provide a stronger causal test, but the present findings remain informative with appropriately limited claims.
(3) The neural findings support category level information with limited mechanistic specificity

The shift toward "bridge-related category information" is appropriate because the decoder distinguishes faces from buildings. It cannot identify reinstatement of the particular B item linking a given AB-BC pair. The association with inference success is meaningful, but category imagery, retrieval strategy, and item-specific recollection are not dissociated. Nor does this association establish that the decoded activity is necessary for inference or mediates stress-related impairment. Despite the response letter's clarification, the abstract and conclusion still describe rapid bridge-element reactivation as an essential or causal mechanism. Consistent category-level, correlational language would align these passages with the analyses. The claim that retrieval practice prevents the theta reduction is also tentative: the reported within-experiment tests and overall, between-experiment comparison do not directly test a stress-by-practice interaction for theta (Section 3.6).
(4) Retrieval specific and item specific benefits remain unresolved

The lack of a matched restudy or additional-exposure condition limits conclusions about the distinctive contribution of retrieval practice. The authors now acknowledge this appropriately. They also explain that practice responses cannot be reliably scored, so the proposed successful-versus-unsuccessful practice analysis is unavailable. The new participant-and-triad mixed-effects model is a useful robustness check, but its interaction is uncertain (p = .058), and it cannot establish whether protection follows successful retrieval of particular items or a broader change in strategy. These limitations remain unresolved by the new model.
Summary:

Guo et al. investigate how acute stress affects memory-based inference and whether retrieval practice protects against these effects. Across two experiments involving 136 participants, the authors report that stress impairs inference performance and alters rapid neural reactivation of bridge-related memories. Retrieval practice appears to preserve both inference performance and the associated neural reactivation.
Strengths:
(1) Two independent experiments strengthen confidence in the behavioral findings.
(2) Time-resolved EEG decoding provides valuable temporal information about bridge-related memory reactivation during inference.
(3) The findings connect a practical learning strategy with behavioral and neural measures of resilience to acute stress.
Weaknesses:

(1) The physiological interpretation requires some clarification. Although the manuscript acknowledges that cortisol was not measured, wording referring to a confirmed cortisol peak remains. The timing reflects an expected physiological response rather than a measured peak, and the available measurements cannot distinguish the respective contributions of glucocorticoid and adrenergic activity.
(2) Significant comparisons in Figures 4 and 6 remain difficult to identify in the supplied revised manuscript. Clear annotations and corresponding legend definitions would improve interpretation.

The authors have acknowledged these concerns in their response, but the corresponding revisions are not fully reflected in the manuscript provided. These remaining issues can be addressed through minor revisions.
Appraisal and Impact

This study provides evidence linking stress-related impairment in memory-based inference to altered rapid reactivation of bridge-related memories. The combination of behavioral experiments and time-resolved EEG offers insight into the processes supporting inference under stress. The finding that retrieval practice can preserve performance and associated neural reactivation is relevant to cognitive neuroscience and applied learning research.
Summary:

In this study, Guo and colleagues investigated the effects of stress and retrieval practice on memory inference. In the first experiment, they found that memory inference was significantly worse after induced stress. Conversely, when participants received retrieval practice in the second experiment, they found no significant differences between these conditions. They monitored EEG during the inference phase and applied multivariate decoding analysis to examine evidence of neural reactivation. Complementing the behavioural findings of the first experiment, they found that they were able to decode the stimulus category of the inference item with more fidelity in the no stress condition. Surprisingly, they found the opposite direction when participants had retrieval practice, with stronger evidence of reactivation in the stress condition than in the control condition.
Strengths:
(1) With a basis in strong theoretical frameworks, the authors have carefully designed two studies investigating the effects of stress and memory retrieval on memory inference.
(2) The use multivariate decoding on the inference phase data combined with behavioural data sheds new light on how stress and retrieval may impact the neural signatures of inference processing.
Weaknesses:

(1) In places, some clarifications are needed about their statistical approach. For example, no multiple comparisons corrections have been applied to the follow-up tests even though they should be considered within the same 'family'. Therefore, the results from the uncorrected analyses should be interpreted with caution, but this should not affect the main claims of the paper.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: (1) Insufficient evidence that retrieval practice specifically protects inference rather than strengthening associative memories

body.p: Sorry for the writing led to misunderstanding,we did not aim to argue that retrieval practice protects inference without affecting associative memories. Instead, we found associative memories mediated the effect of retrieval practice on A-C inference. Specifically, we added an exploratory mediation analysis to quantify the extent to which strengthened premise memory accounted for the association between retrieval practice and later A-C inference. Retrieval practice was associated with better AB/BC premise-memory performance (a = 2.13), and premise-memory performance predicted A-C inference after retrieval practice was controlled (b = 0.012). The bootstrapped indirect effect was significant (ab = 0.026, 95% CI [0.005, 0.049]), while the direct effect of retrieval practice remained significant (c' = 0.028, 95% CI [0.002, 0.055]). We have added this analysis to Section 3.2.3, “Retrieval practice enhanced direct memory retrieval but not baseline inference,” in the revised manuscript. Thus, premise memory (i.e., AB/BC memory) partially, but not completely, mediated the association. Because premise memory was assessed after inference with a 2AFC test, we explicitly describe this analysis as exploratory and interpret it cautiously.

disp-quote.p: (2) Importantly, the direct memory retrieval test used a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) format, which inherently allows a substantial proportion of correct responses to arise from guessing. Consequently, trials classified as 'successfully retrieved' may still include weak associative memory traces, making it difficult to conclude that failures in inference reflect deficits in integration rather than incomplete associative learning.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer1 that A correct response in a 2AFC test is not equivalent to unequivocal retrieval of a strong associative trace. We therefore replaced wording such as 'recalled' or 'successfully retrieved' with the more precise phrase 'answered correctly' when referring to the AB/BC direct-memory test. We also added this limitation to the Methods(2.2.6 Memory inference phase)and clarified that restricting the analysis to both-correct AB/BC trials reduces, but does not eliminate, uncertainty due to guessing. The revised Discussion notes that future studies should use cued recall, confidence ratings, or continuous measures of premise-memory strength to distinguish incomplete associative learning from a deficit in integration more sensitively.

disp-quote.p: (3) Apparent below-chance inference performance raises interpretational concerns

body.p: Thank you for identifying this ambiguity. We did not present the raw ACC in the figure,therefore, the presented value cannot be compare to 0.33 to get above/below chance conclusion. Figure 4A displayed the primary normalized/conditional inference measure, which relates successful A-C performance to the availability of the directly learned AB/BC premise associations; it is therefore not a raw 3AFC proportion and should not be compared directly with 0.33. We revised the Figure 4 legend to define the plotted measure explicitly and to state that it does not represent raw 3AFC accuracy.

disp-quote.p: (4) Between-experiment implementation of retrieval practice weakens causal inference

body.p: We admit that experiment 2 was conducted as a follow-up experiment after Experiment 1, and the retrieval-practice factor was therefore not randomized within a single fully crossed experiment. Although the two experiments were closely matched in recruitment, participant population, laboratory setting, EEG system, task structure, and experimenter team, cohort-related confounds cannot be excluded. We have accordingly revised causal wording throughout the manuscript, described the cross-experiment interaction as an association, and added this limitation to the Discussion. We also state that a within-experiment 2 x 2 design (Stress x Retrieval Practice) is needed to provide stronger causal evidence.

disp-quote.p: (5) Lack of an appropriate comparison condition limits the interpretation of retrieval-practice mechanisms

body.p: The present study did not include a re-exposure or restudy control condition. Therefore, the current design cannot determine whether the observed effect was specifically attributable to retrieval practice or could also be produced by re-exposure or restudy. We have added this limitation to the Discussion and noted that future studies should include a re-exposure or restudy control condition to clarify the specific contribution of retrieval practice.

disp-quote.p: (6) Furthermore, it is unclear whether retrieval practice operates at the trial level or the participant level. Retrieval practice could enhance memory representations for specific practiced items, making those trials more resistant to stress, or it could induce a more global change in cognitive strategy or stress resilience across participants. One way to address this issue would be to analyze inference performance separately for trials that were successfully retrieved during the retrieval practice phase versus those that were not

body.p: We agree with reviewer1 that additional analyses of retrieval performance during retrieval could help improve. However, in Experiment 2, retrieval practice was implemented using a free-recall procedure. Because participants' responses during this phase were not recorded, retrieval-practice performance could not be reliably coded for individual AB/BC associations. Consequently, the present data do not allow us to compare later A-C inference performance between associations that were successfully versus unsuccessfully retrieved during retrieval practice.

As an indirect robustness check, we fitted a mixed-effects model to trial-level A-C inference accuracy, including fixed effects of stress, retrieval practice, and their interaction, as well as random intercepts for participants and ABC triads. The stress-by-retrieval-practice interaction showed a positive trend consistent with the participant-level analysis, although it did not reach the conventional significance threshold (b = 0.116, SE = 0.061, z = 1.90, p = .058). We have added this analysis to Section 3.2.3, “Retrieval practice enhanced direct memory retrieval but not baseline inference,” in the revised manuscript. Future studies should adopt a standardized retrieval-practice procedure and systematically record retrieval-practice performance for each association. This would allow researchers to determine whether the protective effect of retrieval practice is specific to successfully retrieved trials or reflects a broader participant-level effect.

disp-quote.p: (7) Interpretation of EEG decoding as bridge-element reactivation may be overstated

body.p: Yes, our decoding targeted at category classification, therefore, we cannot sure specific picture (i.e., the bridge-element was reactivated). We revised the terminology throughout the manuscript to use “bridge-related category information” (or equivalent category-level wording) and removed claims that the analysis decoded a specific bridging memory.

disp-quote.p: (1) The authors correctly timed the inference task to begin approximately 20 minutes after the onset of the stressor. While this window aligns with the expected peak of the glucocorticoid (HPA) response, it also represents a period where the rapid adrenergic (SAM) response, confirmed by heart rate elevation, is still highly influential. As the authors acknowledge, because they did not collect saliva samples due to safety protocols, they cannot definitively separate the influence of peak cortisol from the tail-end of the adrenergic surge on the observed memory impairments.

body.p: The approximately 20-minute interval was selected on the basis of prior stress-and-retrieval studies and corresponds to the expected window of the delayed HPA response, while the heart-rate data also indicate that autonomic arousal remained relevant. Saliva collection was omitted because the study was conducted under COVID-19 safety protocols, and the present data therefore cannot dissociate glucocorticoid from adrenergic contributions. We revised the manuscript to avoid implying that cortisol was measured or that a cortisol peak was confirmed, and we now state explicitly that future studies should collect hormonal measures, when safe, to separate these mechanisms.

disp-quote.p: (2) Figures 4 and 6: Without asterisks is really difficult to compare the significant group differences.

body.p: Thank you for this suggestion, we added asterisks to Figures 4 and 6. At the same time, statistical significance was already conveyed in the original figures by whether the confidence intervals included zero.

disp-quote.p: (1) There are some key gaps in the reporting of the data. In particular, data is missing on how many trials were included in the inference phase and how many were retrieved in the direct memory task. This is important to know as the main conclusions are based on inference trials proportional to the direct retrieval trials. Considering that the direct retrieval performance differs significantly between the experiments, there could be issues with floor/ceiling effects (in the behaviour) and statistical power (in the EEG results) that confound the comparisons between experiments. Without the data, it is difficult to draw conclusions.

body.p: We agree with Reviewer 3 and have added Table S1 to the Supplementary Material. The table reports group-level direct-memory correct counts, the number of triads for which both AB and BC were answered correctly, and conditional A-C accuracy. Importantly, the number of both-correct AB/BC triads did not differ significantly between stress and control groups in either Experiment 1 (t (66) = -1.65, p = .10) or Experiment 2 (t(66) = -0.28, p = .78). Moreover, the cross-experiment stress-by-retrieval-practice interaction remained significant after controlling for both-correct triad count (b = 0.051, SE = 0.024, t = 2.17, p = .031, 95% CI [0.005, 0.098]). We have added this analysis to Section 3.2.2, “Retrieval practice protects direct memory retrieval from stress without affecting premise pairs counts. These additions make the available trial numbers transparent and indicate that the primary behavioral pattern was not explained by unequal numbers of premise-supported trials.

disp-quote.p: (2) Additionally, one-tailed t-tests have been used in follow-up tests, and, as I understand it, no multiple comparisons corrections have been applied to the post-hoc tests, suggesting that these findings should be interpreted with caution.

body.p: The one-tailed follow-up tests were used because the relevant hypotheses were directional a priori. Based on previous findings and our theoretical framework, we specifically predicted that acute stress would impair inference-related performance and neural reactivation, whereas retrieval practice would mitigate these effects. These follow-up tests were therefore planned comparisons used to decompose the significant omnibus effects in the predicted directions, rather than exploratory post-hoc comparisons. For this reason, we considered one-tailed testing appropriate. Similarly, we did not apply an additional multiple-comparison correction to these planned follow-up tests because they were limited in number, theory-driven, and designed to evaluate specific directional predictions rather than to search broadly across multiple possible contrasts. Importantly, our conclusions do not depend on any single follow-up comparison, but on the consistent pattern observed across behavioral inference performance, neural decoding of bridge-related category information, and theta-band activity. We have revised the manuscript to clarify the rationale for these analyses.

disp-quote.p: (3) In places, the structure is unclear, making the narrative difficult to follow, often making it necessary for the reader to go back and forth between the sections to understand the study and analyses.

body.p: We thank Reviewer 3 for this helpful suggestion. We have thoroughly reorganized the manuscript based on the detailed recommendations to improve the overall narrative flow and readability, ensuring that the study and its analyses are easy to follow.

disp-quote.p: (1) There is no mention of why the delay between learning and test is important. The delay may relate to consolidation, but the rationale is unclear.

body.p: We added the rationale for the using the 24-hour delay between learning and test to the Introduction. First, separating Day 1 learning/retrieval practice from Day 2 stress induction and testing minimizes direct effects of stress on encoding and aligns the design with prior work on stress-related impairment of delayed retrieval (Kuhlmann et al., 2005; Schönfeld et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2016). Second, the delay allows the longer-term advantage of retrieval practice to emerge; prior work showed that repeated study can be advantageous on an immediate test, whereas retrieval practice produces better retention after longer delays (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). The interval therefore permits assessment of memory after offline processing, sleep, and natural forgetting. We also state explicitly that consolidation was neither manipulated nor measured here, so the design cannot establish that consolidation caused the stress-buffering effect.

disp-quote.p: (2) Additionally, it is unclear what happened between Day 1 and Day 2 (did you ask the participants to do anything between the sessions, e.g., refrain from alcohol, sleep at a normal time, if so, was this recorded, etc?).

body.p: Participants received no additional task, intervention, or behavioral restrictions between sessions, and alcohol use and sleep schedules were not recorded. They returned to the laboratory approximately 24 hours after Day 1 under otherwise naturalistic conditions. We added this information explicitly to the Experimental Procedure section. We agree that monitoring sleep and substance use would improve control over potential intersession variability in future studies.

disp-quote.p: (3) Section 2.5 Time-frequency analyses: The rationale for investigating theta power is unclear. Did the authors only investigate theta, or were other frequency bands often associated with memory retrieval also explored (e.g., alpha or beta)? If so, these should be reported. If not, the rationale should be clearer

body.p: We clarified that theta was selected a priori because theta oscillations have been linked to associative memory, retrieval, hippocampal-prefrontal communication, and memory integration in associative-inference paradigms (including Backus et al., 2016). The time-frequency analysis therefore focused on theta power (2-8 Hz) rather than conducting an exploratory search across frequency bands. Alpha and beta bands were not analyzed, and this is now stated explicitly in the Methods. In the Discussion, we now relate the theta-band findings to the behavioral and decoding results, noting that acute stress reduced theta power during the later stage of inference, whereas retrieval practice prevented this reduction and enhanced theta activity during the earlier stage of inference.

disp-quote.p: (4) 2.6.2 Analysis of Memory Inference Performance: There seems to be a disconnect between the hypothesis, which predicts that Experiment 2 conditions will be the same (i.e., confirming the null) and the independent t-test, which would tell you if the alternative can be accepted (rather than if it's a true null). Bayes or Equivalence tests would instead link to the hypothesis

body.p: Because a non-significant frequentist t-test cannot directly provide evidence for the null hypothesis, we additionally conducted a Bayesian independent-samples t-test. The analysis yielded BF10 = 0.361 (BF01 = 2.77), providing evidence in support of the null hypothesis that memory inference performance did not differ between the stress and control groups in Experiment 2. We have added this analysis to the Methods and Results.

disp-quote.p: (5) Line 508: It is not clear where the 207 +/- 50 ms time window came from.

body.p: Thank you for identifying this error. The value 207 ms was a typographical mistake and the correct value is 198 ms. We rewrote the procedure in detail 2.6.4 Optimal time window identification and validation). In short, participant-level peak latencies were first identified in the localizer training data; their group mean was 197.46 ms (SD = 245.22 ms), which was rounded to define the primary 198 +/- 50 ms training window. An independent cross-task time-generalization analysis yielded a peak latency of 246.01 ms (SD = 220.08 ms). This did not differ significantly from the localizer-derived latency, t(133) = 1.66, p = .10, supporting use of the fixed 198 +/- 50 ms window. The Methods now describe all three steps and the corrected value consistently.

disp-quote.p: (6) Section 3.5: It is not quite clear to me why the choice phase is of interest for the decoder. As I understand it, the participants are asked to select the image during this 3-second time window, meaning that they will be moving (artifacts). Therefore, I am unsure what question this analysis is addressing and would recommend clarification

body.p: We clarified that our primary theoretical interest was in the pre-choice inference period, during which participants considered and integrated the relevant information before making a response. We were also interested, secondarily, in the choice period to examine whether bridge-related category reactivation persisted into response selection. Thus, the inference period served as our primary neural window of interest, with the choice period providing a complementary analysis.

We agree that button presses create a risk of movement-related contamination. EEG trials were visually inspected, and ICA was used to remove ocular and movement-related components; nevertheless, we now interpret the choice-period findings cautiously.

disp-quote.p: (7) The title boldly suggests that the restoration of the impairment is due to memory reactivation. Although the evidence hints that this may be the case, there could be many other factors contributing to the results, and the title can be misleading. I would therefore recommend changing the title to suggest a link with memory reactivation.

body.p: Thank you for this suggestion. We have revised the title to “Retrieval practice prevents stress-induced inference impairment and preserves rapid bridge-related memory reactivation” to avoid implying a causal role of memory reactivation.

disp-quote.p: Figure 1A: illustrates the stimuli as words, whereas the stimuli were images. To avoid confusion, I would recommend replacing the words with images (or adding images alongside).

body.p: We have replaced the words with images in Figure 1A to accurately reflect the stimuli used in the experiment.

disp-quote.p: Line 654: I presume the authors meant to say "memory inference phase" instead of "memory reference phase".

body.p: Sorry for that. We apologize for this typographical error. We have corrected “memory reference phase” to “memory inference phase.”

body.p: For the remaining minor comments, we have made the corresponding revisions throughout the manuscript. To keep the response letter focused on the major scientific issues and avoid an overly lengthy point-by-point description of minor editorial changes, we do not elaborate on each of these changes here. All corresponding revisions can be found in the revised manuscript.
